narrative:
The 2017 Detroit Tigers entered the season carrying the final embers of a dynasty that had burned brightly for nearly a decade. With Miguel Cabrera aging, the pitching staff fraying, and the front office quietly beginning to acknowledge a rebuild was inevitable, Detroit tried to squeeze one more competitive season out of a roster that was visibly running out of time. They broke even in April at 12-12, a record that masked genuine turbulence — closer Francisco Rodríguez was already a liability in high-leverage situations, surrendering key runs in back-to-back early appearances, while unlikely heroes like Andrew Romine (a grand slam) and Mikie Mahtook provided the kind of unexpected lift that kept the team from sinking outright.

May and June told a story of slow erosion. The Tigers went 13-16 and 10-15 in those months, and the bullpen became a recurring wound. K-Rod's continued struggles, combined with shaky outings from Justin Wilson and others, meant leads were never truly safe. Still, flashes of the team's offensive potential surfaced — Tyler Collins hit a go-ahead three-run homer in May, and Cabrera delivered a timely two-run blast in June. The team was competitive enough to frustrate, but not quite good enough to sustain anything. The trade deadline loomed, and with it, a reckoning about what this roster actually was.

July marked the inflection point. Mikie Mahtook's stunning go-ahead home run on July 19th provided one of the season's most electric moments, only for Justin Wilson to immediately squander it with a catastrophic blown save — a microcosm of the whole year. Days later, Bruce Rondón gave up a three-run homer to Josh Reddick in Houston. The organization responded by selling at the deadline, shipping Wilson and others out of town. Justin Upton delivered two of the season's most positive plays in August, including a grand slam and a go-ahead two-run shot, offering a final reminder of what this lineup could do. But the pitching staff was beyond repair.

September was a free fall. A 6-23 record in the final month was one of the worst collapses in baseball, a dispiriting march through meaningless games that effectively doubled as an audition for the rebuild to come. Alex Wilson gave up a grand slam to Jed Lowrie in Oakland. Drew VerHagen was torched in late September. The only grace note was a Mikie Mahtook single in mid-September that drove in a run during an otherwise bleak stretch. The 2017 Tigers finished 64-98, a franchise nadir, and the closing of a competitive era. The ghosts of Verlander, Scherzer, and those deep playoff runs had fully faded. A new chapter — patient, painful, and uncertain — was about to begin.

chapters.title: Treading Water
chapters.description: Detroit breaks even in April, surviving early bullpen misfires with timely heroics from unexpected sources.

chapters.title: Slow Bleed
chapters.description: May and June bring a losing record and mounting bullpen failures, though Cabrera and Collins provide occasional sparks.

chapters.title: The Breaking Point
chapters.description: July's dramatic swings — from Mahtook's go-ahead homer to Wilson's immediate implosion — force the front office into a teardown at the trade deadline.

chapters.title: Upton's Last Stand
chapters.description: Justin Upton provides two of the season's biggest offensive moments in August, offering a final showcase of the team's fading firepower.

chapters.title: September Collapse
chapters.description: A catastrophic 6-23 September — punctuated by grand slams surrendered and late-game implosions — closes the book on Detroit's competitive era.
